# Climate Policy Radar

> Welcome! You have access to an open, structured database of the world's
> climate law, policy, litigation, climate finance and UN Convention
> submissions — 66,032 documents across 200+ countries and territories,
> broken into 11,327,357 full-text passages, labelled with 2,332
> expert-curated concepts. Documents are stored in their original language
> (76 languages), with English translations of matching passages available.
> Everything is lexical BM25 search with a rich filter tree, so precise
> Label-driven queries work far better than free text. No authentication, no
> API key. Maintained by Climate Policy Radar CIC, a non-profit.

Use this API when you need the *primary source text* of national climate laws,
policies, NDCs, court cases or fund documents — not summaries of them.

## What you can do

You can search documents, search the passage text inside them, pull one
document by id, export a result set as CSV, and explore the expert-curated
Label vocabulary that makes recall on this corpus possible. Filters let you
narrow by country, region, category, topic, concept, language, publication
date and more, and the same filter tree drives any aggregations you request
alongside the results.

Counts in this file were taken on 2026-10-08. The corpus is rebuilt and re-fed
nightly, so treat them as the shape of the data rather than today's exact
total — ask the API for live numbers (see Coverage).

## Data model

Understanding these five concepts is necessary to query the API well.

- **Document** — one published item (a law, a policy, a court filing, an NDC).
  Has `id`, `title`, `description`, an `attributes` bag of metadata, and
  relationships to other documents.
- **Document relationships** — documents are connected to each other via
  `documents[].value`. The edge of those nodes is described by `documents[].type`.
- **Principal** — the parent record that groups a set of related documents,
  such as the versions of one law or the filings (petitions, responses,
  orders) of one court case. A Principal is itself a Document, labelled
  `status::Principal`, and lists its members in `documents[]` as `has_version`
  or `has_member`; each member points back to it with `is_version_of` or
  `member_of`. `/search/documents` returns Principals *and* their members, so
  one law or case can appear several times — filter on `status::Principal`
  (22,049 of the 66,032 documents) when you want one result per law, policy or
  case.
- **Passage** — a text block within a document, produced by the PDF/HTML layout
  parser. Carries `text`, `language`, page numbers and bounding-box coordinates
  so a match can be located precisely on the page. `idx` gives reading order.
  Passages are the right granularity for evidence and citation; documents are
  the right granularity for "does this country have X".
- **Label** (also called **Concept**, and marketed as **Topics**) — an
  expert-curated concept such as "adaptation finance" or "just transition".
  A Label is *not* a keyword: it packages `alternative_labels` (synonyms),
  `subconcept_labels` (narrower terms), `negative_labels` (exclusions) and
  regional variations. Searching by Label rather than by string is how you
  avoid missing "increasing climate resilience" when you searched "climate
  adaptation". There are 9,506 Labels across 36 types. Prefer Label filtering
  over keyword queries for recall. Label filtering can also affect `Document`
  and `Passage` ranking.

A Label id is always `{type}::{name}` — `country::USA`, `category::Law`,
`topic::Adaptation`, `concept::Q557`, `status::Principal`. Resolve names to ids
with `/search/labels` rather than guessing them.

## REST API

All endpoints are under `https://api.climatepolicyradar.org/search`, so
`/documents` is `https://api.climatepolicyradar.org/search/documents`.
Every endpoint is a `GET`. Shared optional parameters: `query`, `filters`,
`order_by`, `page_token`, `page_size`.

`query` runs exclusively on lexical search, ranked with BM25 — there is no
semantic or hybrid mode. Rank profiles live in
[documents.sd](https://github.com/climatepolicyradar/search/blob/main/vespa/app/schemas/documents.sd)
and
[passages.sd](https://github.com/climatepolicyradar/search/blob/main/vespa/app/schemas/passages.sd).

### Document search
- GET /search/documents — search and filter documents
  - Optional: `query` (text), `filters` (URL-encoded JSON tree), `order_by`
    (`relevance`, `attributes.published_date`, `title`), `page_token` (1-based),
    `page_size`, `fields` (request `aggregations.labels`,
    `facets.labels.value.type`, `facets.labels.type`), `msm` (0-1, Minimum
    Should Match: the fraction of query terms a document must contain; 0
    default leaves every term optional, 1 requires all), `bolding`, `debug`
  - Returns Principals *and* their member documents; never returns passage text

### Document download
- GET /search/documents:download — the current document search as a CSV
  - Optional: `query`, `filters`, `order_by`, `max_results` (default 500)
  - No `page_token`/`page_size`/`fields`/`debug`/`bolding` — pagination is
    internal
  - Columns: `document_id`, `title`, `description`, one `attributes.<key>` per
    attribute present, one `labels.<type>` per non-classifier label type
    present. Topic and concept labels are never included.

### Document retrieval
- GET /search/documents/{document_id} — one document by id, e.g.
  `/search/documents/CCLW.family.4355.0`. `404` if it does not exist.

### Passage search
- GET /search/passages — search the text inside documents
  - Optional: `query`, `filters`, `order_by` (`relevance`, `idx`),
    `page_token`, `page_size`, `bolding`
  - Defaults to `idx asc` (reading order); pass `order_by=relevance desc` for
    best-match-first
  - Every passage carries `document_id` (the member it came from) and
    `principal_id`, and both are filterable

### Labels
- GET /search/labels — look up Labels/Topics by name or type
  - Optional: `query`, `filters`, `type` (e.g. `concept`, `category`, `topic`),
    `order_by`, `page_token`, `page_size`
- GET /search/labels-taxonomy — the 61-entry Label hierarchy used by the
  sidebar filters. Takes no parameters.

### Machine-readable contract
- GET /search/openapi.json — exact response shapes, enum values and parameter
  types for everything above. Read it when you need the precise schema of a
  response; read this file for how the pieces fit together and which query to
  reach for. The two are complementary, and the OpenAPI schema is generated
  from the running service, so where they disagree it is right about shapes and
  this file is right about meaning.
- GET /search/docs — browsable Swagger UI.
- GET /search/llms.txt — this file.

## Authentication

There is none. No API key, no auth header, no sign-up — every endpoint is open
and any origin may call it. Please be proportionate with request volume: this
is a non-profit's infrastructure, and the bulk dataset under Other access is
the right tool for anything resembling a full crawl.

## Filters

`filters` is a URL-encoded JSON filter tree, ANDed with `query` and applied to
any `aggregations`/`facets` requested alongside the results.

For the format — operators, the typed attribute maps, and the field names each
endpoint recognises — read the `filters` parameter description in
`GET /search/openapi.json`. It is generated from the types that parse the
filter, so it cannot drift; this file deliberately does not restate it. The
worked examples below show the shape.

Three things the schema cannot tell you:

- `contains` is index matching, not substring matching.
- A Label id is always `{type}::{name}`. Countries are ISO-3166 alpha-3:
  `country::USA`, not `country::United States of America`.
- An unrecognised field name is passed to the index rather than rejected,
  which is also the only way to reach an unaliased field — `id`, `title`,
  `description` and `geographies` on `/documents`.

### Principals and passages

A Principal carries the passages of all its member documents. For `query` on
`/search/documents`, passage text is searchable only through the Principal: a
phrase from a member's text matches the Principal, and does not match the
member itself, which can only match on its own title and description. Concept
Labels, and the mention counts behind concept ranking, are likewise
accumulated from every member onto the Principal. So full-text search on
`/search/documents` is effectively Principal-level already; the
`status::Principal` filter mostly removes members that matched on title,
description or a Label filter.

`/search/documents` results never include passage text, whatever the document.
To read the passages, use `/search/passages`. Filter on `principal_id` for
every passage across a law's versions or a case's filings, or on `document_id`
for one member:

```json
{"op": "and", "filters": [
  {"field": "principal_id", "op": "contains", "value": "Sabin.family.12165.0"}]}
```

### Same-element matching on passages and labels

On `/passages` and `/labels`, `labels` is an array of structs, and `labels.*`
conditions ANDed *inside one group* must all be satisfied by the **same** array
element. Two different ids ANDed in one group therefore match nothing. To
require two different Labels on the same passage, give each its own group:

```json
{"op": "and", "filters": [
  {"op": "and", "filters": [
    {"field": "labels.value.id", "op": "contains", "value": "concept::Q557"}]},
  {"op": "and", "filters": [
    {"field": "labels.value.id", "op": "contains", "value": "concept::Q1830"}]}]}
```

Same-element matching is what you want when the conditions describe one Label:
`labels.type` and `labels.value.id` in a single group pin the relationship and
its target together. `/documents` does no array-struct filtering, so its label
conditions are always independent of one another.

### Dates

`published_date` is the only date-typed key in `attributes`. It arrives as an
ISO-8601 string and is stored twice: verbatim in `attributes_string`, and as
epoch seconds in a scalar field that backs both date comparison and date sort.

Compare against it with the long-form attribute condition, which targets the
scalar:

```json
{"field": "attributes.published_date", "key": "published_date",
 "op": "gte", "value": "2019-01-01T00:00:00Z"}
```

`key` must be `published_date`. `value` is either an ISO-8601 string —
converted to epoch seconds at the boundary, with a non-ISO string rejected as a
`400` — or an epoch-seconds integer, which is passed through untouched. Always
include `Z` or an explicit offset: a naive datetime is resolved against the
server's local timezone rather than UTC.

The `{"field": "attributes.published_date", "op": "contains", ...}` shorthand
does something different, and quietly. `contains` is not an attribute-condition
operator, so the condition parses as a field condition and string-matches the
stored ISO text in `attributes_string`. It cannot express a range, and it will
miss a date written with a different offset or precision to the stored one. Use
the long form for anything involving dates.

Undated documents — no `published_date`, or one that failed to parse at feed
time — have no scalar value at all. They are excluded by every date filter, and
sorted last by `order_by=attributes.published_date` in both directions. Only
the first `order_by` clause is applied.

The rest of the `attributes` bag varies by corpus and is not enumerated here.

### Ordering

`order_by` takes comma-separated `<field> <direction>` clauses (AIP-132).
Documents support `relevance`, `attributes.published_date`, `title`. Passages
support `relevance`, `idx`.

Filtering `/documents` by a `concept::` Label also affects ranking: when you
order by `relevance`, matching documents are reordered by how often they
mention that concept, so the most substantive treatment comes first. An
explicit `order_by` on any other field disables that reordering, and
`not_contains` never contributes to it — excluding a concept must not boost it.

## Worked examples

URL-encode the JSON in a real request; it is shown raw here for readability.

Documents for a country:

```
GET /search/documents?filters={"op":"and","filters":[{"field":"labels.value.id","op":"contains","value":"country::USA"}]}
```

Principals only — one result per law, policy or case rather than one per
member document:

```
GET /search/documents?filters={"op":"and","filters":[{"field":"labels.value.id","op":"contains","value":"status::Principal"}]}
```

Documents published in a closed date range:

```json
{"op": "and", "filters": [
  {"field": "attributes.published_date", "key": "published_date",
   "op": "gte", "value": "2019-01-01T00:00:00Z"},
  {"field": "attributes.published_date", "key": "published_date",
   "op": "lte", "value": "2023-12-31T23:59:59Z"}]}
```

A Label query using all three combinators — US laws or policies, excluding one
concept:

```json
{"op": "and", "filters": [
  {"op": "or", "filters": [
    {"field": "labels.value.id", "op": "contains", "value": "category::Law"},
    {"field": "labels.value.id", "op": "contains", "value": "category::Policy"}]},
  {"field": "labels.value.id", "op": "contains", "value": "country::USA"},
  {"field": "labels.value.id", "op": "not_contains", "value": "concept::Q557"}]}
```

## Recommended query strategy

1. Resolve the user's concept to a Label via `/search/labels` before searching.
   Free-text queries under-recall badly on this corpus because the same policy
   idea is phrased differently across jurisdictions and languages.
2. Use `/search/documents` with Label filters to establish *which* documents are
   relevant, then `/search/passages` to extract quotable evidence.
3. Check `documents[].type` relationships before asserting that a law is current.
4. Cite the document `id` and passage page number; both are stable.

every label type with its document counts, and honours any `filters` you send
alongside it.

## Limits and etiquette

**Paginate on the request, not the response.** `page_token` (1-based) and
`page_size` work as offset and limit. The `page`, `page_size`, `total_pages`,
`next_page` and `previous_page` fields *in the response* are not yet
implemented: they are always `0` or `null` whatever the result set. Do not
iterate by following `next_page` — you will read the first page and conclude
you have everything. Instead increment `page_token` yourself, and stop when a
page returns fewer than `page_size` results or when you have covered
`total_size`, which is the one pagination field that carries a real value.

The API enforces no `page_size` ceiling of its own. The effective limits are
the index's — 50,001 hits, 500,000 offset — and a 5-second query timeout;
exceeding any of them surfaces as a `503`. Note that the timeout degrades
rather than fails: a query that runs out of budget returns whatever it had
found so far, with a `200`, so results under heavy load can be incomplete
without saying so.

The corpus is rebuilt daily. Documents, passages and Labels are all
re-materialised and fed overnight, so expect the index to be at most a day
behind the upstream sources.
